content: Aquagenic pruritus is a dermatological condition characterized by the onset of intense, prickling-like itching of the skin. This itching occurs without any visible skin lesions and is triggered by contact with water, regardless of its temperature. Symptoms can manifest immediately after exposure to water or humid air and may persist for an hour or longer. Other potential triggers include sweating or exposure to blowing air. The condition appears to affect individuals of all genders and ages equally. In some cases, aquagenic pruritus may be a symptom of underlying conditions such as Primary Polycythemia or Polycythemia Vera. This disorder should not be underestimated, as the severity of the itching can significantly disrupt daily activities, limit bathing, and frequently lead to severe depression. The term aquagenic pruritus is derived from Latin, with aquagenic meaning water-induced and pruritus meaning itch. Treatment options for aquagenic pruritus include the application of capsaicin cream to the affected areas and ultraviolet-B phototherapy. Some individuals use tanning beds as a form of phototherapy, but frequent tanning raises concerns about the risk of skin cancer. Since pruritus is sometimes thought to be mediated by histamine, antihistamines such as H1 blockers (e.g., Claritin) and H2 blockers (e.g., Cimetidine) may provide relief. However, symptoms may recur after each exposure to water and can persist for years. Many individuals manage the itching by turning the shower water to a hot setting for the last five minutes of bathing or by applying heat to the skin immediately after showering using heating pads or hair dryers. Additionally, wearing cotton clothing and using cotton bedding can help prevent itching or provide relief for some sufferers.
